clue.text: Old military bands

parts.note: not musical bands of soldiers but strips of cloth that soldiers once wound round their lower legs from ankle to knee

explanation.surface: A nostalgic mention of regimental brass bands from years gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bands' suggests music; here it means strips of cloth, as worn wrapped round the shins by soldiers in the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Puttees were long cloth strips wound spirally round the leg, standard army kit in the early twentieth century.

clue.text: Turning last to big game? The horses!

indicators.note: turning the word last about rearranges its four letters

parts.note: lions are classic big game, the large animals hunted on safari

explanation.surface: At the end of a safari, someone switches from big game to horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning' usually signals a reversal, but here it means turning the letters over into a new order, an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Stallions are male horses kept for breeding, a particular kind of horse.

clue.text: Fleet of limb, the girl

parts.note: an arm is a limb
Ada is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl described as fast on her feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet' looks like the adjective meaning swift; it is the noun, a group of ships.
explanation.definitionFit: An armada is a large fleet of warships, most famously the Spanish one of 1588.

clue.text: Infallible casting of rune by group

indicators.note: casting runes means throwing them, so the letters of the word rune are thrown into a new order

parts.note: a ring is a group, as of conspirators or dealers

explanation.surface: A gang of fortune-tellers casting runes and getting it right every time.
explanation.walkthrough: Runes are cast like dice by fortune-tellers, so 'casting' fits the surface while signalling a rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unerring never makes a mistake, which is what infallible means.

clue.text: Working in the mines, or not fully so?

explanation.surface: A wry look at miners' jobs, asking whether they are fully occupied.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first part as 'under' plus 'employment': work done below ground. The second is the economist's word for work that uses too little of a person's time or skill.
explanation.definitionFit: Mining is a job done below ground, playfully an under-ground job, while the economic term means working fewer hours than one wants or below one's skills.

clue.text: Lamb is easy to cook, by the way

indicators.note: cooking a dish turns its ingredients into something new, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A recipe note: lamb is simple to cook, mentioned in passing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lamb' looks like meat, which 'to cook' supports; it is Charles Lamb, the English essayist. 'to cook' rearranges IS EASY into ESSAYI.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Lamb wrote the Essays of Elia, so he is a celebrated writer of essays.

clue.text: Game of golf with the canon?

explanation.surface: A clergyman joining in for eighteen holes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canon' suggests a cathedral clergyman; it is the musical form in which voices enter in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A round is one complete game of golf, and also a song for voices entering one after another, a simple kind of canon.

clue.text: Appearance of these weeds exasperates

explanation.surface: A gardener annoyed at seeing stinging plants spring up.
explanation.definitionFit: Stinging plants are a familiar weed, and to rile someone is to irritate them as those stinging leaves do.

clue.text: Piano out of tune, right? Could be better

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, soft

indicators.note: out of tune means wrong, so the letters of the word tune are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A complaint about a piano that is out of tune and needs improving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be better' sounds like faint criticism; read it as 'could be a bettor', someone who places bets. 'out of' rearranges TUNE as UNTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A punter is someone who gambles on horses, a bettor.

clue.text: Squally wind from Pluto repels

parts.note: Dis is another name for Pluto, Roman god of the underworld
gusts are the sudden blasts of a squally wind

explanation.surface: Stormy weather from the dwarf planet drives things away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pluto' suggests the planet; crosswords use it for the god, also called Dis.
explanation.definitionFit: To disgust someone is to sicken them so that they recoil, which is to repel them.

clue.text: Note girl taking the lead's star quality

definitions.note: the clue gives a noun phrase; the answer is the adjective meaning having that quality, star-shaped

indicators.note: the girl takes the lead, coming in front of the note rather than after it as the clue reads

parts.note: Stella is a girl's name
te is the seventh note of the tonic sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A girl leading the cast shows the charisma of a true star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'star quality' sounds like charisma; it means the quality of being star-shaped. Stella is also Latin for star.
explanation.definitionFit: Stellate is the botanist's word for radiating like the points of a star, a shape quality.

clue.text: One does it in the mountains to call toboggan back?

definitions.text: One does it in the mountains
definitions.note: a clause describing what someone does, matching the answer as a verb

parts.note: yo is a call used to attract attention

indicators.note: brought back here means the word sled is read in reverse order

parts.note: a sled is a toboggan

explanation.surface: Someone shouting across a mountainside to get a sledge returned.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a clause, 'one does it', so the answer is the verb: what one does in the mountains is yodel. 'back' turns the toboggan word round.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpine herdsmen sing with rapid switches between chest voice and falsetto, a practice of mountain regions.

clue.text: Take a break — the tea is poured out

indicators.note: tea poured out leaves its pot, and these letters leave their order and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tea break announced as the cups are filled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poured out' rearranges the eight letters of THE TEA IS.
explanation.definitionFit: To pause before acting, holding off for a moment, is a short break in what one does.

clue.text: Doubt corrosion must follow condensation

indicators.note: corrosion must come after condensation, so it is placed second

parts.note: mist is water vapour condensed into fine droplets
rust is the corrosion of iron

explanation.surface: A doubtful engineer's warning that rust follows damp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must follow' puts the corrosion word after the condensation word, though the clue names it first.
explanation.definitionFit: Mistrust is a lack of trust, a suspicion akin to doubt.

clue.text: Troops right to capture coffin-bearer going over the lines?

definitions.note: a phrase for a person who goes over lines, standing for the agent noun

indicators.note: the troops and right together take the coffin-bearer captive, holding it between them

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, are troops of the British Army
a hearse is the vehicle that bears a coffin

explanation.surface: Soldiers given the right to seize a funeral vehicle crossing the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going over the lines' suggests crossing battle lines; it means an actor running through a script.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor learning a part repeatedly practises the script, so one who practises lines is a rehearser.

clue.text: Right inside sepulchre, a single instrument found

indicators.note: the right letter goes inside the word for the sepulchre

parts.note: a tomb is a sepulchre
one means a single

explanation.surface: An archaeologist discovers a lone instrument inside a tomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sepulchre' is a burial place; the 'found' at the end is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A trombone is a brass musical instrument with a sliding tube.

clue.text: Did he send notes down from the gallery?

definitions.text: Did he send notes down from the gallery?

parts.words: Did he send notes down from the gallery?
parts.note: not a spectator dropping messages but a medieval musician playing in the raised gallery of a great hall, sending musical notes down to the diners

explanation.surface: A question about someone passing messages down from a balcony.
explanation.walkthrough: Old halls had a raised gallery where hired musicians played during feasts; the notes are musical ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Medieval entertainers who sang or played for a lord's household performed from a gallery named after them.

clue.text: Nice tax might produce it, but it wouldn't be right

definitions.note: a clause about something wrong, standing for the adjective meaning not correct

indicators.note: rearranging the letters of the words nice tax could produce something new

explanation.surface: A complaint that a pleasant-sounding tax would still be unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might produce' rearranges NICE TAX; 'right' here means accurate, not morally just.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inexact is not precisely correct, so it is not right in the sense of accurate.

clue.text: With excitement have a go at it, flying around

indicators.note: letters flying around land in a different order, so the words a go at it are shuffled

explanation.surface: Encouragement to try something while rushing about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flying around' rearranges A GO AT IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitato is an Italian musical direction telling the player to perform in an agitated, restless way.

clue.text: Take precedence over one given order to exit, say?

indicators.note: say means the words are spoken and heard as a word of the same sound

parts.note: the exit is the way out, and given a new order its two words become out way

explanation.surface: Someone who has been told to leave is put ahead of others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given order' looks like a command; it means put in a different order. WAY OUT, the exit, becomes OUT WAY, and 'say' turns that into a word of the same sound.
explanation.definitionFit: When one consideration outweighs another it counts for more and so comes first.

clue.text: Just the thing for the traveller?

definitions.text: Just the thing for the traveller?

parts.words: Just the thing for the traveller?
parts.note: plays on an idiom meaning exactly what is wanted, while a passenger literally needs a travel pass to board

explanation.surface: A recommendation of some handy item for anyone on a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'just the ticket' means exactly the right thing, and a traveller does literally need one.
explanation.definitionFit: A pass bought for a journey is what a passenger needs, and the idiom makes it the ideal item.

clue.text: First side led off then second brought back — though not often

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of the word side is used
off means wrong or out of place, so the letters of the word led are rearranged
brought back means the word for a second is read backwards

parts.note: mo is a short informal word for a second, a moment

explanation.surface: A cricket or football report: one team led, then the other came back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges LED to ELD, and 'brought back' reverses MO to OM.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done seldom happens rarely, only now and then.

clue.text: Academic, in another word, right — with aridity increasing

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the comparative adjective, more dry

parts.note: Dr, doctor, is the title of an academic with a doctorate
ie, id est, means that is, introducing the same thing in other words

explanation.surface: A scholar rephrasing a point about a desert getting drier.
explanation.walkthrough: IE stands for id est, Latin for 'that is', used to put something in other words.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of dry describes something becoming more arid.

clue.text: From mountaintop, expert gathers speed — it's steep!

parts.note: the top of the word mountain is its first letter, M
an ace is an expert
rate means speed

explanation.surface: A skier racing down from the summit of a very steep slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'steep' reads as an adjective for the slope; it is the verb meaning to soak.
explanation.definitionFit: To macerate food is to soften it by soaking in liquid, which is to steep it.

clue.text: Writer dressed in old king's underwear

indicators.note: dressed in means the writer's name is put inside the king's, as if clothed by it

parts.note: Old King Cole is the merry monarch of the English nursery rhyme
Kingsley and Martin Amis are English novelists

explanation.surface: A novelist clothed in some old monarch's undergarment.
explanation.walkthrough: Old King Cole is the 'merry old soul' of a British nursery rhyme. 'dressed in' places the writer inside the king's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A camisole is a woman's loose sleeveless undergarment for the upper body.

clue.text: Makes use of hybrid trees — unspecified number

indicators.note: a hybrid is a cross, a mixture, so the letters are mixed together

parts.note: x stands for an unknown or unspecified number in algebra

explanation.surface: A forester growing an indefinite number of crossbred trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hybrid' mixes TREES with X into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To exert influence or strength is to bring it to bear, putting it to use.

clue.text: Most bleak seen from vessel in first sea trial

indicators.note: first means just the opening letter of the word sea
the vessel sits in the word for trial

parts.note: a test is a trial
an ark is a vessel, as Noah's

explanation.surface: A grim view from the deck of a ship on its maiden sea trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the vessel inside the trial, and the first letter of 'sea' goes in front; 'seen from' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Stark means harsh and desolate, so its superlative is the most desolate or bleak.
